title: A serious health risk shouldn’t be regulated like an ordinary product
explanation: Products such as vapes sit at the intersection of commerce, addiction, harm reduction, and youth protection. Treating them exactly like ordinary consumer goods ignores nicotine dependence, respiratory exposure, advertising effects, and the risk of early initiation. At the same time, regulation should distinguish evidence about adult smoking cessation from marketing that normalizes use among minors. Effective policy can include age controls, product standards, taxation, packaging rules, advertising restrictions, and enforcement.
why: The Philippines has a young population and a large digital advertising environment. Weak regulation can allow health risks to spread quickly before long-term consequences are fully visible.

title: Never underestimate a mother’s love for her child
explanation: Filipino motherhood is often described through sacrifice, but romanticizing sacrifice can hide the physical, emotional, and economic burden placed on mothers. Care work includes pregnancy, breastfeeding, childcare, household management, emotional labor, income generation, and often elder care. Love is powerful, but families and institutions should not assume mothers can absorb unlimited responsibility without support.
why: Policies on maternity care, childcare, workplace flexibility, reproductive health, social protection, and paternal responsibility determine whether motherhood is supported or simply celebrated in words.

title: Dito sa Albay, hindi lang ulan ang bumabagsak — kundi abo rin
explanation: Living near an active volcano such as Mayon means residents must manage multiple hazards, including ashfall, lahars, pyroclastic flows, heavy rain, and evacuation. Ash can affect breathing, water, agriculture, roofs, machinery, and transport. Disaster planning therefore requires hazard maps, monitoring, evacuation routes, masks, livestock planning, and communication that accounts for both volcanic and weather conditions.
why: Millions live near volcanoes and other geologic hazards. Albay demonstrates why disaster preparedness must be continuous, locally understood, and linked to livelihoods rather than activated only when an eruption becomes dramatic.

title: ABSOLUTE CINEMA: When silver screens lose their luster
explanation: Philippine cinemas face pressure from streaming, high ticket prices, production costs, limited screens, changing audience habits, and competition from global content. Local filmmakers also struggle with financing, marketing, distribution, and short theatrical windows. Cinema policy is therefore not only about artistic grants; it involves the economic ecosystem that determines whether Filipino films reach viewers and recover their costs.
why: A weak film industry reduces creative jobs, cultural exports, and the ability of local stories to compete for public attention. Film is both culture and an industry.

title: When truth-telling means you’re an ‘NPA’
explanation: Red-tagging occurs when individuals or organizations are labeled or insinuated to be linked with communist armed groups without sufficient evidence or due process. Journalists, activists, lawyers, church workers, teachers, and community organizers have raised concerns that such labeling can expose people to harassment or violence. Government has legitimate security responsibilities, but accusations must be evidence-based and legally accountable.
why: When criticism can be treated as proof of insurgency, public debate narrows. Protecting lawful dissent strengthens democracy while allowing genuine security cases to be pursued through proper investigation.

title: Even the ‘most disciplined city’ is not safe for journalists.
explanation: A city’s branding around order or discipline does not automatically guarantee press freedom. Journalists may still face intimidation, legal threats, access restrictions, political pressure, online harassment, or physical danger. Media safety depends on institutions, accountability, independent courts, professional standards, and a political culture that tolerates scrutiny.
why: Local journalism is often the first to uncover problems involving mayors, police, contracts, disasters, and public services. If reporters fear retaliation, communities lose a critical accountability mechanism.

title: CAUSE OF DISASTER: Was ‘The Rise’ Monterrazas project the reason behind Cebu’s Tino flood
explanation: Flood disasters are rarely caused by a single factor. Extreme rain, slopes, drainage capacity, land-use change, construction, soil conditions, watershed alteration, and blocked waterways can interact. When a major development is blamed, the correct approach is to examine hydrological studies, permits, engineering design, environmental compliance, rainfall data, and independent expert analysis rather than rely on viral claims alone.
why: Rapid urban development is occurring in flood-prone areas across the country. Transparent environmental assessment is necessary to determine when development increases risk and who should be accountable.

title: DAVAO DEGREES: Living in an archipelagic oven
explanation: Extreme heat in Philippine cities is intensified by climate change, humidity, dense construction, limited tree cover, concrete surfaces, traffic, and the urban heat-island effect. Heat affects more than comfort; it can reduce learning, productivity, sleep quality, and cardiovascular safety while increasing electricity demand. Outdoor workers and low-income households without air-conditioning face the greatest exposure.
why: Heat adaptation needs shade, trees, cooling centers, water access, building standards, adjusted work and school schedules, and urban design, not simply more electric fans.

title: It is never about what she wears
explanation: Sexual violence is caused by perpetrators and abusive power, not by a victim’s clothing. Victim-blaming shifts attention away from consent, coercion, age differences, grooming, exploitation, and offender responsibility. In cases involving minors, the power imbalance is even clearer because children cannot be treated as responsible for adult sexual misconduct.
why: Victim-blaming discourages reporting and allows offenders to escape scrutiny. Better education on consent, child protection, grooming, and survivor-centered justice can improve prevention and reporting.

title: Who you see online shapes who you vote offline
explanation: Political bloggers, influencers, creators, fan pages, and algorithmic feeds can shape how voters interpret candidates before official campaigns reach them. Repetition, humor, parasocial trust, short-form video, and selective framing can make political claims feel familiar even when evidence is weak. Online visibility can therefore function as political power.
why: The Philippines is highly active on social media. Voters need to distinguish reporting, commentary, paid promotion, coordinated propaganda, and personal endorsement when judging political information.

title: PASSport PoWHERe?: Why there are closed doors in open skies
explanation: International travel is not equally accessible even when flights are available. Visa rules, passport strength, proof-of-funds requirements, travel history, employment status, immigration screening, and discrimination can determine who can cross borders easily. Mobility is therefore partly a privilege created by geopolitics and economic inequality.
why: Many Filipinos travel for work, family, study, and tourism. Understanding visa systems and migration rules helps explain why a passport is not merely an identity document but a gatekeeper to opportunity.

title: When healthcare becomes a privilege, not a right
explanation: A legal right to health becomes meaningful only when services are available, affordable, geographically reachable, and of acceptable quality. A patient may technically be covered yet still face medicine shortages, long travel distances, specialist scarcity, or indirect costs such as missed work. Health equity therefore requires financing, workforce planning, primary care, referral systems, and local capacity.
why: Poor households often delay treatment until illness becomes severe. Closing access gaps can prevent both avoidable deaths and catastrophic household debt.

title: A nation that can read — but not understand
explanation: Literacy is not simply the ability to pronounce words. Functional literacy includes understanding meaning, evaluating information, following instructions, using numbers, and applying knowledge in real situations. Students may be promoted through grade levels while carrying unresolved comprehension gaps that later affect work, civic participation, and further learning.
why: Reading comprehension affects everything from medicine labels and contracts to online misinformation and job training. Foundational learning is a national productivity issue.

title: NOT JUST WORDS: The Journalist’s Creed beyond NSPC
explanation: Journalism values such as truth, fairness, independence, public service, verification, and accountability should not be treated as ceremonial lines recited at competitions. Student journalists face the same ethical tensions as professionals: pressure from institutions, deadlines, sources, audiences, and personal bias. A creed matters only when it guides difficult decisions.
why: Campus journalism can shape the next generation of reporters and informed citizens. Ethical habits formed early influence the quality of the future information ecosystem.

title: Who controls the campus press?
explanation: Control over student media can come through budgets, appointment of advisers, approval requirements, access to facilities, disciplinary rules, or the threat of withholding recognition. Even without explicit censorship, dependence on administrators can create self-censorship. Editorial independence therefore requires clear governance safeguards.
why: Universities are supposed to develop critical thinking. A campus that celebrates debate while controlling its press sends students a contradictory lesson about democracy.

title: This is what happens when flood control is taken seriously
explanation: Effective flood management combines drainage maintenance, pumping, river restoration, retention areas, land-use regulation, garbage management, early warning, engineering, and transparent project implementation. No single project can eliminate flood risk, especially during extreme rainfall, but systematic planning can substantially reduce exposure and recovery time.
why: Flood-control spending is enormous and politically sensitive. Citizens should judge projects by measurable performance, maintenance, procurement transparency, and whether they reduce risk rather than by ribbon-cuttings.

title: EDSA Unfinished: A victory still being written
explanation: The 1986 People Power Revolution removed an authoritarian government and restored democratic institutions, but democracy is not a one-time event. Corruption, dynasties, inequality, disinformation, human-rights concerns, and weak institutions can persist after a political transition. EDSA is therefore both a historical victory and an unfinished institutional project.
why: Remembering EDSA only as nostalgia misses its larger lesson: political freedom requires continuous defense through institutions, civic participation, and historical truth.

title: WATCH THE SKY: Why the crescent moon determines the start of Ramadan
explanation: The Islamic lunar calendar is based on moon cycles, so the beginning of Ramadan is traditionally connected to the sighting or calculation of the new crescent. Practices can vary among religious authorities and countries depending on methodology. Because a lunar year is shorter than a solar year, Ramadan moves through different seasons over time.
why: Islam is a major part of Philippine history and national life, especially in Mindanao. Understanding Ramadan helps reduce religious ignorance and supports respectful schools, workplaces, and public institutions.

title: PRICE TAG: How corruption slows down economic growth
explanation: Corruption increases the cost of doing business, distorts procurement, directs money toward politically connected projects, discourages investment, weakens competition, and reduces the quality of public services. The economic damage is not limited to stolen money; it includes roads not built properly, classrooms delayed, contracts inflated, and trust eroded.
why: Every peso lost to corruption can mean higher taxes, worse services, weaker infrastructure, or greater debt. Anti-corruption is therefore an economic growth strategy, not just a moral campaign.

title: LOVE, EXPLAINED: How Valentine’s Day became a tradition
explanation: Valentine’s Day evolved through religious traditions, European romantic customs, commercial culture, greeting cards, flowers, media, and global consumer marketing. In the Philippines it has been localized through mass weddings, school traditions, gift-giving, dining, and social media. Its meaning now ranges from romance to friendship and commercial celebration.
why: Traditions are rarely static. Understanding how global customs become Filipino shows how culture adapts, commercializes, and acquires new local meaning.

title: TESTING ACCOUNTABILITY: The stories behind impeachment complaints lodged vs PBBM
explanation: Impeachment complaints against a president must be evaluated through constitutional grounds, evidence, filing rules, political support, and House procedure. Multiple complaints do not automatically prove wrongdoing, but repeated filings can reveal continuing political or legal disputes. The process is designed to prevent both arbitrary removal and impunity.
why: Impeachment is one of the strongest constitutional accountability tools. Understanding how complaints advance or fail helps citizens distinguish serious cases from political signaling.

title: WHERE YOUR PESO GOES: Unprogrammed appropriations and why they matter
explanation: Unprogrammed appropriations are budget items that can be released only when specified funding conditions are met, such as excess revenue or new financing. They can provide flexibility for urgent or contingent needs, but large amounts raise concerns about transparency, legislative intent, and executive discretion. The key issue is when and how these funds become available.
why: Budget design determines which services are actually funded. Technical categories can hide major policy choices, so taxpayers benefit from understanding where discretionary spending power sits.

title: LEARNING BEHIND: Why most Filipino students never reach proficiency
explanation: Students can advance through school without mastering foundational reading, mathematics, science, or problem-solving when curricula move faster than learning recovery. Teacher shortages, large classes, poverty, language transitions, absenteeism, weak early childhood preparation, and repeated disruptions can compound over years. By senior high school, gaps may be too large to fix with short interventions.
why: A learning crisis affects wages, competitiveness, innovation, and social mobility. The country cannot solve it merely by adding subjects or extending school years without measuring actual mastery.

title: BURIED IN WASTE: Warnings ignored before the Binaliw landfill disaster
explanation: Landfills can become disaster sites when waste slopes, drainage, methane, rainfall, engineering controls, and surrounding settlement are poorly managed. Communities near dumpsites may face odor, pests, contaminated water, fires, landslides, and health risks. A disaster is often preceded by warning signs that require monitoring and regulatory enforcement.
why: Waste management is a local-government responsibility with life-and-death consequences. Proper segregation, engineered disposal, environmental compliance, and community protection are essential.

title: Sinugdanan sa Sulog: How Sinulog became Cebu’s grandest festival
explanation: Sinulog combines religious devotion to the Santo Niño with dance, procession, local history, tourism, commerce, and civic identity. Its movement evokes the current of water, while its modern festival form developed through both religious tradition and organized cultural programming. The event has become a major symbol of Cebu.
why: Festivals are not simply entertainment. They carry faith, local identity, livelihoods, heritage, and political choices about whose history is represented.
